tests.title: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: Logic is the study of correct reasoning, and its father is considered to be:
questions.explanation: Aristotle developed the first formal logic (syllogisms).

questions.question_text: A statement (proposition) is:
options: A sentence that is either true or false
questions.explanation: It makes a claim about the world.

questions.question_text: Which is NOT a proposition?
questions.explanation: Commands, questions and exclamations are not propositions.

questions.question_text: An argument is:
options: A set of statements in which premises are offered in support of a conclusion
questions.explanation: It aims to establish a claim by reasons.

questions.question_text: Premises are _____, and the conclusion is _____:
options: The reasons or evidence; the claim being supported
questions.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises.

questions.question_text: Premise indicators include "because", "since" and "as", and conclusion indicators include:
questions.explanation: They signal the structure of an argument.

questions.question_text: In "Because it is raining, the match will be cancelled," the premise is _____ and the conclusion is _____:
options: The match will be cancelled; it is raining
It is raining; it is raining
It is raining; the match will be cancelled
questions.explanation: "Because" introduces the premise.

questions.question_text: In "Sales rose since we cut prices, so cutting prices works," the conclusion is:
questions.explanation: "So" indicates the conclusion.

questions.question_text: Deductive reasoning is:
options: Reasoning from specific cases to a general probable conclusion
Reasoning from general premises to a specific conclusion that necessarily follows, e.g., "All humans are mortal; Socrates is human; so Socrates is mortal"
questions.explanation: If the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.

questions.question_text: Inductive reasoning is:
options: Reasoning from specific observations to a general, probable conclusion, e.g., "The sun has risen every day, so it will rise tomorrow"
questions.explanation: The conclusion is probable, not certain.

questions.question_text: Abductive reasoning is:
options: Inferring the most likely explanation for an observation
questions.explanation: E.g., a wet road suggests it has rained.

questions.question_text: Deductive reasoning differs from inductive reasoning in that deductive reasoning:
options: Gives certain conclusions, while inductive gives probable conclusions
questions.explanation: Deductive moves from general to specific.

questions.question_text: An argument is valid if:
options: The conclusion follows logically from the premises, and sound if it is valid and all premises are true
questions.explanation: Soundness requires both validity and true premises.

questions.question_text: A valid but unsound argument is:
options: "All birds can fly; penguins are birds; so penguins can fly."
"All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal."
questions.explanation: The logic is valid but the first premise is false.

questions.question_text: A cogent inductive argument is one that:
options: Is strong and has true premises
questions.explanation: It is the inductive equivalent of soundness.

questions.question_text: A syllogism is:
options: A deductive argument with two premises and a conclusion (major premise, minor premise, conclusion)
questions.explanation: Example: All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; so Socrates is mortal.

questions.question_text: The four categorical propositions A, E, I and O are:
options: All S are P; No S are P; Some S are P; Some S are not P
No S are P; All S are P; Some S are not P; Some S are P
All S are P; Some S are P; No S are P; Some S are not P
Some S are P; All S are P; No S are P; Some S are not P
questions.explanation: They are universal affirmative, universal negative, particular affirmative and particular negative.

questions.question_text: "Some managers are not leaders" is an example of:
questions.explanation: It is particular negative.

questions.question_text: "All managers are leaders; Anita is a manager; therefore Anita is a leader" is:
options: Valid (and sound only if the first premise is true)
questions.explanation: The conclusion follows from the premises.

questions.question_text: "All birds fly; penguins are birds; so penguins fly" is:
questions.explanation: The first premise is false.

questions.question_text: A rule of a valid categorical syllogism is that:
options: The middle term appears in the conclusion
Any two premises give a conclusion
The middle term must be distributed at least once, and no conclusion can follow from two negative premises
questions.explanation: Also, a negative premise requires a negative conclusion.

questions.question_text: Modus ponens is: "If P then Q; P; therefore Q." An example is:
options: "If it rains, the road is wet; it doesn't rain; so the road isn't wet."
"If it rains, the road is wet; it rains; so the road is wet."
"If it rains, the road is wet; the road is wet; so it rains."
"It rains or the road is wet."
questions.explanation: It affirms the antecedent.

questions.question_text: Modus tollens is: "If P then Q; not Q; therefore not P." An example is:
options: "If it rains, the road is wet; it rains; so the road is wet."
"If it rains, the road is wet; the road isn't wet; so it didn't rain."
"It rains or the road is wet."
"If it rains, the road is wet; the road is wet; so it rained."
questions.explanation: It denies the consequent.

questions.question_text: A hypothetical syllogism is:
options: "If P then Q; if Q then R; therefore if P then R"
"P or Q; not P; therefore Q"
questions.explanation: It chains conditional statements.

questions.question_text: A disjunctive syllogism is:
options: "P or Q; not P; therefore Q"
"If P then Q; if Q then R"
"If P then Q; P; therefore Q"
questions.explanation: It eliminates one option.

tests.title: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: Affirming the consequent is a fallacy, e.g.,:
options: "If it rains, the road is wet; the road is dry; so it didn't rain."
"If it rains, the road is wet; the road is wet; so it rained."
"If it rains, the road is wet; it rains; so the road is wet."
questions.explanation: The road could be wet for other reasons.

questions.question_text: Denying the antecedent is a fallacy, e.g.,:
options: "If it rains, the road is wet; the road is dry; so it didn't rain."
"If it rains, the road is wet; it didn't rain; so the road isn't wet."
"If it rains, the road is wet; it rained; so it is wet."
questions.explanation: The road may be wet for other reasons.

questions.question_text: Logical connectives include:
options: And, or, not, if…then and if and only if
questions.explanation: They combine statements.

questions.question_text: "P → Q" (if P then Q) is false only when:
options: P is false and Q is true
P is true and Q is false
questions.explanation: All other cases are true.

questions.question_text: "P and Q" is true:
options: Only when both P and Q are true
questions.explanation: It is false if either is false.

questions.question_text: "P or Q" (inclusive) is false:
options: Only when both P and Q are false
questions.explanation: It is true if at least one is true.

questions.question_text: "Not P" is true when:
questions.explanation: Negation reverses the truth value.

questions.question_text: "If P then Q" with P false and Q true is:
questions.explanation: The conditional is false only with a true antecedent and false consequent.

questions.question_text: A necessary condition is one that _____, and a sufficient condition is one that _____:
options: Guarantees the outcome; must be present
Must be present for the outcome; guarantees the outcome
questions.explanation: Oxygen is necessary for fire; a lit match in dry grass is sufficient.

questions.question_text: Critical thinking is:
options: The ability to analyse and evaluate information objectively; skills include analysis, inference and evaluation
questions.explanation: It involves questioning assumptions.

questions.question_text: Socratic questioning is:
options: A method of asking probing questions to examine ideas and assumptions
questions.explanation: It stimulates critical thinking.

questions.question_text: Logic is used in business decision making to:
options: Evaluate options, avoid fallacies and justify decisions
questions.explanation: It supports sound analysis.

questions.question_text: "Every company I have worked with delays payments, so all companies delay payments" is:
questions.explanation: It generalises from limited cases.

questions.question_text: "All banks are regulated by RBI; SBI is a bank; so SBI is regulated by RBI" is:
questions.explanation: It moves from a general rule to a specific case.

questions.question_text: A formal fallacy is an error in _____, and an informal fallacy is an error in _____:
options: The logical structure of the argument; content, language or relevance
questions.explanation: Affirming the consequent is formal; ad hominem is informal.

questions.question_text: The ad hominem fallacy is:
options: Attacking the person instead of the argument, e.g., "You can't trust his plan; he is a failure."
questions.explanation: The person's character is irrelevant to the argument's merit.

questions.question_text: The straw man fallacy is:
options: Misrepresenting an opponent's argument to make it easier to attack
questions.explanation: "You want less spending, so you want schools closed."

questions.question_text: A false dilemma is:
options: Presenting only two options when more exist, e.g., "Either you are with us or against us."
questions.explanation: It oversimplifies.

questions.question_text: The slippery slope fallacy is:
options: Claiming that one step will inevitably lead to extreme consequences without proof
questions.explanation: "If we allow one late arrival, soon nobody will come on time."

questions.question_text: An appeal to authority is a fallacy when:
options: An irrelevant or unqualified authority is cited as proof, e.g., a film star endorsing medical advice
An expert in the field is cited
questions.explanation: The authority must be relevant.

questions.question_text: The bandwagon fallacy is:
options: Claiming something is true or good because many people believe or do it
questions.explanation: "Everyone uses it, so it must be best."

questions.question_text: Circular reasoning (begging the question) is:
options: An argument whose conclusion is already assumed in its premise, e.g., "The Bible is true because it says so"
questions.explanation: It goes round in a circle.

questions.question_text: A red herring fallacy is:
options: Introducing an irrelevant topic to divert attention from the issue
questions.explanation: "Why worry about pollution when there is poverty?"

questions.question_text: Hasty generalisation is:
options: Drawing a general conclusion from a small or unrepresentative sample
questions.explanation: "My two employees were late, so all staff are lazy."

questions.question_text: The post hoc fallacy is:
options: Assuming that because B followed A, A caused B
questions.explanation: "Since the CEO changed, profits fell, so the CEO caused it."

tests.title: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: An appeal to emotion is a fallacy when:
options: Emotions replace logical reasons, e.g., "Think of the poor children if you reject this."
questions.explanation: Emotion should support, not replace, evidence.

questions.question_text: Tu quoque ("you too") is:
options: Rejecting criticism by pointing out the critic's own faults
questions.explanation: "You tell me not to smoke, but you smoke!"

questions.question_text: An appeal to ignorance is:
options: Claiming something is true because it has not been proven false
questions.explanation: "No one has proved ghosts don't exist, so they exist."

questions.question_text: Equivocation is:
options: Using a word with two meanings in an argument, leading to a misleading conclusion
questions.explanation: "A feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; so a feather cannot be dark."

questions.question_text: The genetic fallacy is:
options: Judging an idea by its origin rather than its merit
questions.explanation: "This idea came from a rival, so it is wrong."

questions.question_text: A loaded question is:
options: A question that contains an unfair assumption, e.g., "Have you stopped cheating?"
questions.explanation: It traps the respondent.

questions.question_text: The fallacy of composition is _____, and the fallacy of division is _____:
options: Assuming what is true of the parts is true of the whole; assuming what is true of the whole is true of the parts
questions.explanation: "Each player is great, so the team is great" is composition.

questions.question_text: The appeal to tradition is:
options: Arguing something is right because it has always been done that way
questions.explanation: "We've always done it this way."

questions.question_text: "You can't trust his budget plan; he was fired from his last job" is:
questions.explanation: It attacks the person.

questions.question_text: "Everyone in the office uses this software, so it must be the best" is:
questions.explanation: Popularity is not proof.

questions.question_text: "Either you support this policy or you hate the country" is:
questions.explanation: It ignores other options.

questions.question_text: "He is guilty because he looks suspicious" is:
options: An appeal to appearance/unsupported assumption (hasty judgement)
questions.explanation: Appearance is not evidence of guilt.

questions.question_text: "Since the CEO changed, profits have fallen, so the CEO is the cause" is:
questions.explanation: It confuses sequence with cause.

questions.question_text: "My friend got a high return from this scheme, so it is risk free" is:
questions.explanation: One case does not prove the absence of risk.

questions.question_text: "If we allow one late arrival, soon no one will come on time" is:
questions.explanation: It predicts a chain of extreme consequences.

questions.question_text: Fallacies can be avoided by:
options: Checking evidence, staying on topic and examining assumptions
questions.explanation: Critical thinking helps.

questions.question_text: Rhetoric is:
options: The art of effective and persuasive speaking or writing
questions.explanation: It aims to influence the audience.

questions.question_text: The classic work "Rhetoric" was written by:
questions.explanation: He identified three modes of persuasion.

questions.question_text: The three rhetorical appeals are:
questions.explanation: They are credibility, emotion and logic.

questions.question_text: Ethos is:
options: An appeal to credibility or character, e.g., "As a doctor with 20 years of experience…"
questions.explanation: It builds trust.

questions.question_text: Ethos is established by:
options: Expertise, honesty, experience and good character
questions.explanation: Credentials and fairness build it.

questions.question_text: Pathos is:
options: An appeal to emotion, e.g., "Think of the children who will suffer"
questions.explanation: It moves the audience to feel.

questions.question_text: Advertisements use pathos by:
options: Using emotional images, music and stories to create feelings
questions.explanation: E.g., happy families.

questions.question_text: Logos is:
options: An appeal to logic and reason, e.g., "Studies show this method reduces costs by 25%"
questions.explanation: It uses facts and evidence.

questions.question_text: Sources of logos include:
options: Facts, statistics, logical reasoning and examples
questions.explanation: They support claims.

tests.title: Unit 6: Logical Thinking: Logic, Rhetoric — Ethos, Pathos and Logos – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: Kairos is:
options: The opportune moment or timing for an argument
questions.explanation: A message must suit the occasion.

questions.question_text: The rhetorical triangle consists of:
questions.explanation: It shows how communication works.

questions.question_text: Rhetorical devices include:
options: Metaphor, repetition, rhetorical question, rule of three and analogy
questions.explanation: E.g., "Veni, vidi, vici".

questions.question_text: The weakness of relying on pathos alone is that it:
questions.explanation: Ethos can be weak if the speaker is unknown; logos can be dry.

questions.question_text: A balance of ethos, pathos and logos is necessary because:
options: Credibility, emotion and logic together make persuasion stronger
questions.explanation: Each supports the others.

questions.question_text: In Martin Luther King Jr.'s "I Have a Dream", the vivid imagery of a better future is mainly:
questions.explanation: It also uses ethos (moral authority) and logos (constitutional promises).

questions.question_text: "9 out of 10 dentists recommend" in a toothpaste ad is mainly:
options: Ethos and logos (expert authority and statistics)
questions.explanation: It cites experts and numbers.

questions.question_text: "As a doctor with twenty years of experience, I advise you to exercise daily" is:
questions.explanation: It uses credibility.

questions.question_text: "Think of the children who will suffer if we do nothing" is:
questions.explanation: It appeals to emotion.

questions.question_text: "Studies show that this method reduces costs by 25%" is:
questions.explanation: It uses data.

questions.question_text: Picture description involves:
options: Observing, organising and describing what you see in order, then interpreting it
questions.explanation: Steps: overview, details, mood and interpretation.

questions.question_text: The foreground, middle ground and background are:
options: The parts of a picture nearest, in the middle and furthest from the viewer
questions.explanation: Describe them in order.

questions.question_text: Phrases used to describe positions in a picture include:
options: "in the foreground", "on the left", "in the background" and "next to"
questions.explanation: They show location.

questions.question_text: Colour symbolism: red often signals _____ and green often signals _____:
options: Danger or passion; nature, growth or safety
questions.explanation: Colours carry meanings that vary by culture.

questions.question_text: A good description of a charity poster with a child holding an empty bowl would:
options: Describe the child, the empty bowl and the mood of hunger, noting the emotional impact
questions.explanation: It captures subject and feeling.

questions.question_text: In the charity poster "Rs 50 feeds a child. Registered NGO.", "Registered NGO" is _____, and "Rs 50 feeds a child" is _____:
questions.explanation: Credibility and a concrete figure.

questions.question_text: A smartwatch advertisement showing an athlete at sunrise would be described as:
options: An athlete running along a beach in golden sunrise light wearing the watch
questions.explanation: It conveys energy and motivation.

questions.question_text: In the smartwatch advertisement, the athlete at sunrise appeals mainly through:
options: Pathos (aspiration and motivation), with logos in the features listed
questions.explanation: It sells a lifestyle.

questions.question_text: A bank's home-loan advertisement showing a happy family would be described as:
options: A smiling family in front of their new home
questions.explanation: It shows the benefit emotionally.

questions.question_text: The home-loan advertisement appeals through:
options: Pathos (family security), ethos (the bank's reputation) and logos (interest rate)
questions.explanation: It combines all three.

questions.question_text: A picture of a polluted river with persuasive appeals would show:
options: Dirty water and dead fish (pathos) with facts on pollution (logos) and an environmental group (ethos)
questions.explanation: It urges action.

questions.question_text: A picture of students planting trees would appeal through:
options: Pathos (hope), logos (benefits of trees) and ethos (a school or NGO)
questions.explanation: It promotes environmental action.

questions.question_text: In a health-insurance advertisement, ethos might be shown by:
options: The insurer's long experience and claim settlement record
questions.explanation: Pathos would be a sick family; logos the coverage figures.

questions.question_text: The effectiveness of an advertisement is evaluated by:
options: Its clarity, appeal, credibility, target audience fit and results
questions.explanation: Does it achieve its purpose?

questions.question_text: Emotional appeal becomes manipulation when it:
options: Exploits fear or guilt to deceive or pressure without honest reasons
questions.explanation: Ethical persuasion respects the audience.
